summary: Reviewed src/server/__tests__/routes/workspaces-health.test.ts against the production route handler (src/server/routes/workspaces.ts) and workspace-health module (src/orchestration/workspace-health.ts). All 11 test assertions are accurate reflections of production behaviour. Key contracts verified: (1) the uninitialized-workspace early-return path in the GET /health handler correctly yields { healthy: true, issues: [] } without invoking checkWorkspaceHealth; (2) MockWorkspaceManager correctly mirrors the real manager's throw-on-unknown-project / return-undefined-on-unknown-workspace contract; (3) all relative imports carry .js extensions; (4) dual cleanup registration (process.on('exit') + after()) follows the project mandatory pattern. No blocking issues found.

comments.note: stubOrchestrator = {} as never is safe here because neither health nor regenerate handlers access the orchestrator object. If a future handler change adds orchestrator access, tsc will not catch the gap until runtime. Consider replacing with a typed cast (e.g., {} as WorkspaceOrchestrator) so tsc surfaces any gap at compile time.

[documentation-forward] The test file header (lines 1-9) describes the two tested endpoints but does not name the production source files being exercised. Adding explicit @see references to src/server/routes/workspaces.ts and src/orchestration/workspace-health.ts would help future contributors navigate from test to implementation instantly.

The mockRequest() destroy() implementation (req.emit('error', new Error('destroyed'))) will throw an unhandled-error-event at runtime if no error listener is attached and destroy() is ever called. Since destroy() is never invoked in the current test suite this is latent-only, but a defensive noop or silent swallow would prevent a hard-to-diagnose failure if a future test accidentally invokes it.
